<!-- The pasted output blocks below were captured from a real run via
     tools/precompute-vignettes.R (sampler progress lines and repeated
     warnings trimmed). Regenerate and refresh the blocks when bayesgrove or
     CmdStan changes; outputs are version-dependent.
     Last refreshed against bayesgrove 0.7.0 / CmdStan 2.39.0. -->

bayesgrove records a Bayesian analysis as a graph of computations plus a log
of decisions. The graph part is familiar from build tools: nodes hold code,
edges hold dependencies, results are cached. The part that makes it
bayesgrove is the review loop on top: fits and checks emit typed diagnostic
*summaries*, summaries raise *obligations*, and a blocking obligation holds
downstream work until you record a *decision* — a choice plus a rationale —
that resolves it. The analysis cannot quietly run past evidence you never
looked at.

This vignette walks the smallest real version of that loop with cmdstanr:
one fit, one posterior-predictive check that fails, the obligation it
raises, the decision that answers it, and the branch that repairs the model.
The chunks use `eval = FALSE` with output pasted from a real run, so the
vignette builds without CmdStan on CI. For the mental model behind the
moving parts, see `vignette("concepts")`; this vignette shows them in
motion.

## A project and a first fit

Every analysis lives in an initialized project: a directory with a
`.bayesgrove/` folder holding the graph, the cache, and the decision log.
`bg_use_cmdstanr()` registers the Stan-backed node kinds, and
`bg_use_default_workflow()` opts into the built-in review pack (register
the backend first, so the pack sees the real node kinds rather than its
generic placeholders).

```{r setup}
library(bayesgrove)

handle <- bg_init(
  path = file.path(tempdir(), "bg-getting-started"),
  project_name = "Getting Started"
)
bg_use_cmdstanr(handle)
bg_use_default_workflow(handle)
```

The data are 50 skewed, strictly positive measurements. We will do what
analysts do all the time: start with a normal model anyway.

```{r data}
set.seed(31)
y <- round(rlnorm(50, meanlog = 0, sdlog = 0.8), 3)
```

`bg_fit_stan()` collapses the minimal lifecycle into one call: it creates a
data node, attaches the data, creates a fit node consuming it, and runs the
fit. The package ships the example Stan programs, so the code below runs as
pasted.

```{r fit}
normal_program <- system.file(
  "stan/normal_iid.stan",
  package = "bayesgrove",
  mustWork = TRUE
)

n_fit <- bg_fit_stan(
  handle,
  stan_file = normal_program,
  data = list(N = length(y), y = y),
  label = "Normal model",
  seed = 21,
  chains = 4
)
```

```
#> Starting run "run_dfbdc04b" with 1 node to execute.
#> Running node "node_66f87a33"...
#> Running node "node_7bd2286f"...
#> <bg_run_handle> run_dfbdc04b
#> • Status: succeeded
#> • Executed Nodes: 2
```

The sampler is happy — no divergences, good R-hats. `bg_status()` shows the
project state, and `bg_next_actions()` asks the workflow pack whether any
evidence demands attention:

```{r first-guidance}
bg_status(handle)
```

```
#> $workflow_state
#> [1] "idle"
#>
#> $runnable_nodes
#> [1] 0
#>
#> $blocked_nodes
#> [1] 0
#>
#> $pending_gates
#> [1] 0
#>
#> $active_jobs
#> [1] 0
#>
#> $last_run_id
#> [1] "run_dfbdc04b"
#>
#> $health
#> [1] "ok"
#>
#> $messages

```

```{r first-obligations}
guide <- bg_next_actions(handle)
guide$obligations
```

```
#> named list()
```

No obligations. That is worth pausing on: an empty answer here is not
"nothing happened", it is a positive statement that every fresh summary in
the project has been reviewed or is unremarkable. So far the only summary is
the clean HMC diagnostic from the fit.

## A check that fails

Clean sampling says the *computation* worked, not that the *model* is any
good. The built-in `ppc` node kind computes posterior-predictive p-values
for a set of test statistics and stores plot-ready draws. It takes two
inputs: the fit (for the `yrep` draws) and the data node (for the observed
`y`). The fit's data node is simply the fit node's input, so we can read it
off the graph:

```{r ppc}
graph <- bg_read_graph(handle)
n_data <- Filter(
  function(edge) identical(edge$to, n_fit),
  graph$edges
)[[1]]$from

n_ppc <- bg_add_node(
  handle,
  kind = "ppc",
  label = "PPC: normal model",
  inputs = c(n_fit, n_data),
  params = list(stats = c("mean", "sd", "min", "max"))
)
run <- bg_run(handle, targets = n_ppc)
```

```
#> Starting run "run_631ca2d5" with 1 node to execute.
#> Running node "node_7ea22ed9"...
```

The p-values compare each statistic of the observed data against its
posterior-predictive distribution. Values near 0 or 1 mean the model cannot
reproduce that feature of the data:

```{r ppc-summary}
ppc_summary <- bg_read_summaries(handle, include_stale = FALSE)
ppc_summary <- Filter(
  function(s) identical(s$summary_kind, "posterior_predictive_check"),
  ppc_summary
)[[1]]
ppc_summary$severity
ppc_summary$metrics
```

```
#> [1] "warning"
#> $max
#> [1] 2e-04
#>
#> $mean
#> [1] 0.5098
#>
#> $min
#> [1] 2e-04
#>
#> $sd
#> [1] 0.5025
```

Both tail statistics give it away, in opposite directions: the model
happily predicts negative values the strictly positive data never show
(`min`), and its thin symmetric tail cannot reach the largest observed
values (`max`). The center is fine — `mean` and `sd` are unremarkable —
which is exactly why a skewed sample can hide behind a normal model until
you check its extremes. One caveat before moving on: posterior-predictive
p-values are conservative tripwires, not calibrated tests — an unremarkable
p-value is weak evidence of fit. The primary check is graphical:

```{r ppc-plot, fig.alt = "Posterior predictive density overlay for the normal model"}
bg_plot(handle, n_ppc)
```

![Posterior predictive density overlay for the normal model](figures/getting-started-ppc-normal.png)

## The obligation, and the decision that answers it

The extreme p-values arrived as a `warning`-severity summary, and the
default pack turns fresh warnings into a blocking obligation — at project
scope it files everything under its baseline review lane,
`review_computation_validity` (the optional packs add more specific
vocabularies):

```{r obligation}
guide <- bg_next_actions(handle)
vapply(guide$obligations, `[[`, character(1), "kind")
vapply(guide$actions, `[[`, character(1), "kind")
```

```
#>                  obl_a969dc96
#> "review_computation_validity"
#>        act_16593cd9        act_ed08cddc
#>   "record_decision" "branch_and_modify"
```

An *obligation* is a demand raised from evidence; each one comes with
suggested *actions* that would resolve it. Blocking obligations also
translate into *holds*: pass them to the planner and any node downstream of
the criticized one stays parked until the review happens.

```{r holds}
held_plan <- bg_plan(handle, external_holds = guide$metadata$external_holds)
held_plan$external_blocked
```

```
#> list()
```

Empty — and instructively so. The failing check is the last node in this
tiny graph, so there is nothing downstream to hold yet. The moment you add
one (a comparison, a report step, a follow-up fit), it lands in
`external_blocked` until the obligation is resolved. The hold mechanism is
how unreviewed evidence stops an analysis from advancing *past* it, not a
punishment for the node that produced it.

To resolve the obligation we record a decision. A decision is a permanent
log entry: the prompt, the choice, the rationale, and the ids of the
evidence it covers. The suggested `record_decision` action carries the right
metadata in its payload, so we do not have to assemble it by hand:

```{r decision}
review <- Filter(
  function(a) identical(a$kind, "record_decision"),
  guide$actions
)[[1]]

bg_record_decision(
  handle,
  scope = "project",
  prompt = "Does the normal model reproduce the data?",
  choice = "reject_normal_model",
  rationale = paste(
    "The observed minimum is far outside the posterior predictive",
    "distribution: the data are strictly positive and right-skewed,",
    "and a normal model cannot express that. Refit on the log scale."
  ),
  kind = review$payload$decision_type,
  metadata = review$payload[c("node_ids", "summary_ids")]
)

bg_next_actions(handle)$obligations
```

```
#> <bg_decision_record> dec_632c0a7b
#> • Prompt: Does the normal model reproduce the data?
#> • Choice: reject_normal_model
#> • Rationale: The observed minimum is far outside the posterior predictive
#>   distribution: the data are strictly positive and right-skewed, and a normal
#>   model cannot express that. Refit on the log scale.
#> named list()
```

The obligation is gone — not because the evidence went away, but because a
recorded judgment now covers it. Both stay in the log: a reviewer can later
see exactly which p-value prompted the rejection and what the stated
reasoning was.

## Branch to the repair

The rationale named the repair: model the log scale. A *branch* keeps the
rejected fit and its criticism in the record while the analysis moves on —
provenance is the point, so we never edit the past. `bg_branch()` copies the
fit node into a new branch; `bg_update_node()` merges params, so only the
Stan program needs swapping. The default pack asks every active branch for
an inferential goal, which doubles as documentation of why the branch
exists.

```{r branch}
branch <- bg_branch(handle, n_fit, label = "Lognormal model")

bg_set_goal(
  project = handle,
  branch_id = branch$branch_id,
  kind = "observable_prediction",
  label = "Positive-valued predictions",
  rationale = "The rejected normal fit motivates a lognormal likelihood."
)

lognormal_program <- system.file(
  "stan/lognormal_iid.stan",
  package = "bayesgrove",
  mustWork = TRUE
)

bg_update_node(
  handle,
  branch$root_node_id,
  params = list(stan_file = lognormal_program)
)
run2 <- bg_run(handle, targets = branch$root_node_id)
```

```
#> <bg_decision_record> dec_ca79d9cb
#> • Prompt: Set inferential goal
#> • Choice: Positive-valued predictions
#> • Rationale: The rejected normal fit motivates a lognormal likelihood.
#> [1] "node_4610511f"
#> Starting run "run_f3475fdc" with 1 node to execute.
#> Running node "node_4610511f"...
```

A second `ppc` node on the branch confirms the repair:

```{r branch-ppc}
n_ppc2 <- bg_add_node(
  handle,
  kind = "ppc",
  label = "PPC: lognormal model",
  inputs = c(branch$root_node_id, n_data),
  params = list(stats = c("mean", "sd", "min", "max"))
)
bg_run(handle, targets = n_ppc2)

ppc2 <- Filter(
  function(s) {
    identical(s$summary_kind, "posterior_predictive_check") &&
      identical(s$node_id, n_ppc2)
  },
  bg_read_summaries(handle, include_stale = FALSE)
)[[1]]
ppc2$severity
ppc2$metrics
```

```
#> Starting run "run_cc95c582" with 1 node to execute.
#> Running node "node_70de7bc7"...
#> <bg_run_handle> run_cc95c582
#> • Status: succeeded
#> • Executed Nodes: 1
#> [1] "ok"
#> $max
#> [1] 0.2
#>
#> $mean
#> [1] 0.4708
#>
#> $min
#> [1] 0.6925
#>
#> $sd
#> [1] 0.3262
```

Both models remain in the graph — the rejected normal fit with its failed
check and the decision that rejected it, and the lognormal fit with a clean
one:

```{r graph}
print(bg_read_graph(handle))
```

```
#> ── Execution Graph ──
#>
#> └── Normal model_data <stan_data> [new]
#>     ├── Normal model <cmdstanr_fit> [new]
#>     │   └── PPC: normal model <ppc> [new]
#>     ├── [already shown: PPC: normal model]
#>     ├── Lognormal model <cmdstanr_fit> [new]
#>     │   └── PPC: lognormal model <ppc> [new]
#>     └── [already shown: PPC: lognormal model]
```

## Where this goes next

This was one turn of the loop on the smallest possible example. The same
mechanics scale up:

- **Computation review.** When HMC itself misbehaves — divergences, low
  E-BFMI — the same loop fires on the sampler diagnostics instead of a
  predictive check. `vignette("eight-schools")` walks that case, including
  the branch-scoped review a repair branch inherits.
- **Comparison and disposition.** With two or more clean candidate fits, the
  default pack demands an explicit comparison (via LOO) and then an
  accept-or-reject disposition for each branch before the analysis can
  conclude. `vignette("case-study-roaches")` runs that full arc on real
  data, from a badly misfitting first model to an exported report.
- **Reporting.** `bg_export_report(handle, format = "md")` renders the whole
  trail — graph, diagnostics, decisions, branch lineage — into a document; a
  `bg_bundle()` archive backs it with the machine-readable logs. See the
  reproducible-research article for what a reviewer can verify from the
  bundle.

## Reference: the pieces individually

The sections above used the machinery in one continuous story. The notes
below are the pieces in isolation, for when you come back looking for one
of them.

### Gates: pre-planned checkpoints

Obligations arise dynamically from evidence. When you know *in advance* that
a step needs sign-off, put a *gate* on the edge instead. A gate blocks
planning until it is answered, and the answer (with its rationale) lands in
the same decision log:

```{r gate}
gate <- bg_add_gate(
  project = handle,
  from = n_data,
  to = n_fit,
  prompt = "Were the measurements validated before modeling?",
  alternatives = c("yes", "no")
)

bg_pending_gates(handle)

bg_answer_gate(
  project = handle,
  id = gate$id,
  choice = "yes",
  rationale = "Values were cross-checked against the collection protocol."
)
```

```
#> $gate_84ce804b
#> $gate_84ce804b$id
#> [1] "gate_84ce804b"

#> $gate_84ce804b$edge_id
#> [1] "edge_2ed4dcc6"

#>

#>

#> • Choice: yes
#> • Rationale: Values were cross-checked against the collection protocol.
```

### Scopes

Obligations and decisions carry a scope: `project` or `branch:<id>`. A
project-scope decision does not silently cover a branch, and vice versa —
each active line of analysis answers for its own evidence. Pass `scope` and
`branch_id` to `bg_next_actions()` to interrogate a specific branch, as the
eight-schools vignette does after branching.

### Freshness

Summaries are fingerprinted against the exact node configuration that
produced them. Change the params, the data, or the Stan program and the old
summary goes *stale*: it stops feeding obligations until the node is rerun.
This is what makes "the checks passed" meaningful across sessions and
machines.

### Additional workflow packs

`bg_use_default_workflow()` installs the built-in starter pack used here.
`bg_use_workflow_packs()` can instead activate an explicit set, such as the
default Bayesian pack shown below plus the optional prior-workflow pack.
These packs add richer review vocabularies while remaining summary-driven:
executors keep returning plain data, and the packs decide what that evidence
obliges.

```{r packs, eval = FALSE}
bg_use_workflow_packs(
  handle,
  c("bayesgrove.default_bayesian", "bayesgrove.prior_workflow")
)
```

### The REPL

`bg_repl(handle)` wraps the same loop in an interactive dashboard: it shows
outstanding obligations, previews the suggested actions, and can execute
them. Everything it does goes through the public API you used above, so a
REPL session and a script leave the same audit trail.

### Extending

Custom node kinds, custom executors (including deterministic mock executors
for testing), template registration, and custom summary kinds are covered in
`vignette("extensions")`. The short version: register an executor that
returns `list(result = ..., summaries = ...)` and the review loop picks up
your evidence exactly as it picked up the built-in checks here.
